cases.message: Why did my score drop from 611 to 588 this month?

routing.reason: The member asks why their score dropped, which is a score-changes question, and utilization is named as a common cause of drops, so it is also relevant.

cases.reply:
That's a frustrating drop to see. Your profile shows your score went from 611 on 2026-09-15 to 588 now (VantageScore 3.0). Two things in your profile likely explain it, biggest first.

**1. A new 30-day late payment.** The retail store card payment due 2026-08-25 was missed and reported 30 days late on 2026-09-28. A new late payment usually has the biggest effect of anything on a report. You paid the past-due amount on 2026-10-02, so the account is current again. That helps from here. If the late payment is accurate, it can stay on your report. If you believe it's wrong, you can dispute it.

**2. Higher utilization (how much of your card limits you're using).** Your balances were reported at $1,410 of $3,000 in limits on 2026-10-05. That's 47%, up from 30% the month before. Common guidance is under 30%, and under 10% tends to be better. By card:
- Retail store card: $900 of $1,500, or 60%
- Bank credit card: $510 of $1,500, or 34%

Utilization is the part you can change fastest. Under most current scoring models, it stops weighing on your score once a lower balance is reported, usually after the next statement. Your overall score still depends on everything else on your report, including the late payment.

Your 10 on-time Credit Builder payments are still working for you. Keeping every payment on time from here matters most.

Next step: Pay down the retail store card before its statement closing date so a lower balance gets reported.

cases.message: I've never missed a payment, so why did my score go down 13 points?

routing.reason: The member asks why their score dropped despite never missing a payment, which is a score-change question; utilization is also a common cause of drops and the utilization skill explicitly covers 'why did my score drop' questions.

cases.reply:
That's a frustrating drop to see when you've paid everything on time. The most likely cause is higher card balances, not anything you did wrong with payments.

**What changed**

Your profile shows your score went from 668 on September 15 to 655 now (VantageScore 3.0). On October 5, your cards reported $2,550 owed out of $3,000 in limits. That's 85% utilization (how much of your card limits you're using), up from 70% the month before. The car repair you charged on September 20 likely pushed that balance up.

Scoring models look at your overall ratio and at each card on its own:
- **Rewards credit card:** $1,900 of $2,000, or 95%
- **Bank credit card:** $650 of $1,000, or 65%

Common guidance is to stay under 30%, and under 10% tends to be better. Both cards are well above that. Your profile shows no late payments, no new hard inquiries, and no new negative items. Your on-time history is still working for you.

**What can help**

- **Pay before the statement closing date.** Card issuers usually report your statement balance, so paying earlier lowers what gets reported.
- **Pay more than once a month** to keep balances lower through the cycle.
- **Focus on the rewards card first,** since it's the one at 95%.

Under most current models, high utilization stops weighing on your score once a lower balance is reported, usually after the next statement. Your overall score still depends on everything else in your report, so I can't say how much it may change. Your Credit Builder plan is a loan, not a card, so it doesn't count toward utilization.

Next step: Look up your rewards card's statement closing date and make a payment a few days before it.

cases.message: A lender told me I don't have a FICO score. How long until I get one?

routing.reason: The member has little or no credit history and asks how long until they have a FICO score, which matches the credit-builder-account skill's scope for thin-file users asking how long until they have a score.

cases.reply:
You don't have a FICO score yet because your credit history is still very new. FICO has two basic requirements before it can create a score:

- **At least one account open for 6 months or more.** Your Credit Builder plan was opened on June 1, 2026, so it's about 4 months old. This is the requirement you're still working toward.
- **At least one account reported to the credit bureaus in the past 6 months.** Your Credit Builder payments are reported every month, so you already meet this one.

I can't give you an exact date when a FICO score will appear, or what it will be. Meeting the minimums lets FICO score your file, but the timing also depends on when the bureaus update your report and which FICO version a lender uses.

You do already have a score. Your profile shows a VantageScore 3.0 of 612, up from 603 on September 15. VantageScore is a different scoring model that can score newer files. That's why you have one even without a FICO score.

The best thing you can do right now is keep your payments on time. You've made 4 on-time Credit Builder payments with no late ones. Each one adds to your history. A payment 30 or more days past due would be reported as late.

Next step: Make your next Credit Builder payment by its due date, November 1, 2026.

cases.message: I've paid rent on time for over two years. Why does Rent Reporting only show 4 months?

routing.reason: The member asks why Rent Reporting shows only four months of history, which falls under the rent-reporting skill covering the add-on's behavior, including adding up to 12 months of past rent.

cases.reply:
Rent Reporting only reports months from when you enrolled, not your full rental history. Your profile shows you enrolled on June 1, 2026, and chose not to add past rent. So June through September are your 4 reported months.

**What about October?** You paid October rent ($1,400) on time on October 1. It hasn't been reported yet, so it isn't counted in your 4 months.

**Can the earlier months be added?** Yes, partly. Your lease started September 1, 2024, but the app can add up to 12 months of past rent, not the full two years. It's a one-time $25 fee, on top of the $4 monthly cost. This adds more positive history to your reports. It can't promise a specific score change.

**Will it count toward your mortgage?** That depends on the lender. The app reports rent to TransUnion and Experian, not Equifax. Some scoring models count rent and others ignore it:

- Your profile score is VantageScore 3.0, which can count rent.
- Many mortgage lenders use older FICO versions that ignore rent.
- Since September 2026, approved lenders may choose VantageScore 4.0 instead, which can count rent.

So whether your rent history helps depends on which score and credit bureaus your lender uses.

Next step: Before you decide on adding past rent, ask a mortgage lender you're considering which score and credit bureaus they use.

cases.message: When will the phone company collection come off my credit report?

routing.reason: The member asks when a phone company collection will fall off their report, which is a collections question about how long collection accounts stay.

cases.reply:
**Your phone company collection should come off your credit report around March 2029.** Your profile shows the original delinquency (the first missed payment that led to the collection) was March 14, 2022. A collection can stay up to 7 years from that date.

**A few things to know:**
- **Paying won't restart the 7-year clock.** If the debt is sold to another collector, the clock doesn't restart either.
- **Paying won't remove it early.** A paid non-medical collection still shows on your report, marked as paid.
- **Paying could still help your score.** Your profile shows a VantageScore 3.0 of 560. That model ignores paid collections. Some lenders use other models, such as FICO 8, which still count them.
- **There's a separate legal deadline.** Each state has its own time limit for suing over a debt, often 3 to 6 years. In many states, a partial payment or written promise to pay can restart it. Before you pay or promise anything, a legal aid office or attorney can check your state's rule. This is general information, not legal advice.

You also got a letter from the collection agency on September 22. If money is tight, you can ask the collector about a payment plan. A nonprofit credit counselor can also help you weigh your options. For questions about your app account, use Help > Chat with support in the app.

Whether to pay is your choice. The 2029 date stays the same either way.

Next step: Find the September 22 letter and check the creditor and balance it lists to confirm they match the $1,200 phone bill.

- If you're upgraded, your $500 deposit is returned.
- The review doesn't promise an upgrade. I don't have details on how long the review takes or exactly when a refund would arrive, so I can't give you a date.

Keep paying on time. Your next Secured Card payment is due November 5, 2026. Your October statement closed with a $60 balance on your $500 limit. That's 12% of the card's limit, and your overall utilization (how much of your total card limits you're using) is also 12%.

If you aren't upgraded, your deposit stays with the account as long as it's open.

cases.message: If I pay my next Credit Builder payment a few days late, will it hurt my score?

routing.reason: The member asks whether a few-days-late Credit Builder payment hurts their score, which is covered by credit-builder-account (late payment effects on the plan) and payment-history (how late payments get reported and impact).

cases.reply:
No. A Credit Builder payment that's 1 to 29 days late is not reported as late to the credit bureaus, so a few days late won't put a late mark on your report.

**How the timing works**
Your profile shows your next payment is due November 1, 2026. It's only reported as late once it reaches 30 or more days past due. To stay safe, make sure it's paid by November 30.

**Why it matters to stay under 30 days**
Payment history (your record of paying on time) is the biggest part of your score. Once a payment hits 30 days late, it's reported as late. That mark can stay on your reports for up to 7 years, and its impact is largest while it's recent.

Right now your profile shows 7 on-time Credit Builder payments and no late payments. That's a strong record worth protecting.

I don't have details on whether a few days late carries a fee. You can check that in Help > Chat with support.

Next step: Set a reminder or turn on autopay for your November 1 payment so it's paid well before the 30-day mark.

cases.message: Should I apply for one of the credit cards I saw in the Marketplace?

routing.reason: The member asks whether to apply for a credit card seen in the Marketplace, which is a marketplace-offers question about whether a new card fits their situation.

cases.reply:
**Applying can be a reasonable choice for you, but only you can decide.** Your profile looks steady: 4 on-time Credit Builder payments, no late payments, no negative items, and no hard inquiries in the last 12 months. Your VantageScore 3.0 is 612, up from 603 last month.

**The tradeoff**
- **What may help:** A card would add revolving credit (a credit line you can reuse) to your file. Right now your only account is an installment plan (fixed payments), so a card could add variety. Its limit would also give you available credit to keep balances low against.
- **What may hurt:** Applying usually triggers a hard inquiry (a credit check that can lower your score for a while). A new account also lowers the average age of your accounts.

**A few things to know**
- The card issuer, not the app, sets the terms and decides on approval. I don't know your approval odds. In September, a lender's check found no FICO score for you yet, and some issuers may look for one.
- Some issuers offer prequalification. It's usually a soft check that doesn't affect your score. It isn't approval, but it can help you see where you stand first.
- If you're denied, the issuer must send a notice with the reasons or explain how to get them.
- Marketplace partners may pay the app when a user is approved.

If you apply, compare the APR (yearly interest rate), fees, and terms on each offer page.

Next step: Open the offer you liked most and check whether it offers prequalification before you apply.

cases.message: How much will the Debt Settlement service cost me for my $2,800 card?

routing.reason: The member asks what the Debt Settlement service costs on a $2,800 card balance, which is covered by the debt-settlement skill's fee of 20% of the amount saved.

cases.reply:
**Right now, it has cost you $0, and you won't owe a fee until a settlement is agreed.** Your profile shows the $2,800 Bank credit card is still in negotiation, with no settlement yet and $0 in fees charged.

**How the fee works**
- The fee is 20% of the amount saved. Amount saved means your $2,800 balance minus the settlement amount.
- It's charged only after a settlement is agreed and you make at least one payment under it. There are no upfront fees.

**An example with your balance (not a prediction)**
If the creditor agreed to settle for $1,800:
- Amount saved: $1,000
- Fee: $200
- Total you'd pay: $2,000

The real number depends on what the creditor accepts. Outcomes vary a lot, and the creditor doesn't have to agree to any settlement.

**Other things to know**
- **Taxes:** Forgiven debt, like the $1,000 in the example, may count as taxable income. A Form 1099-C usually comes when $600 or more is forgiven, but the debt may count even without one. This isn't tax advice, so a tax professional can tell you how it applies to you.
- **Your credit report:** A settled account usually shows as "settled for less than the full balance." It still shows as a charge-off (a debt the lender wrote off as a loss) and stays for its full 7-year reporting period.
- **Collection can continue:** Negotiating doesn't stop the creditor from collecting or suing.
- **Missed payments:** I can't confirm what happens if you miss a payment under a settlement. Human support can tell you (Help > Chat with support).
- **Free options:** You can also negotiate directly with the creditor for free, or get help from a nonprofit credit counselor.

Next step: When an offer comes in, get the full terms in writing before you make any payment or sign anything.

cases.message: How long will the late payment from 2024 stay on my credit report?

routing.reason: The member asks how long a 2024 late payment stays on their report, which is payment-history.

cases.reply:
Your 30-day late payment can stay on your credit report for up to 7 years from the original delinquency date (the date you first fell behind). Your profile shows that late on your Bank credit card, with an original delinquency date of November 12, 2024. So it can stay until about November 2031.

**The impact fades over time.** A late payment hurts most while it's recent. As it ages and you add on-time payments, it counts for less. Your profile shows the card is current now, and your 4 months of on-time rent reporting also add positive history.

**What won't remove it early:**
- Closing the card won't remove it, and it could hurt by lowering your total available credit.
- Since you haven't said the late is wrong, disputing it isn't the right tool. Disputes are only for information that is inaccurate or incomplete.
- No company can force an accurate late off your report early.

**One optional step.** You can send a goodwill letter. This asks the card company to remove the late as a courtesy. It tends to fit a one-time slip on an otherwise clean account like yours. The company doesn't have to agree, so think of it as a request, not a fix.

With a mortgage planned for 2027, the best thing you can do is keep every payment on time from here. Autopay for at least the minimum on the card and auto loan can help with that.

Next step: Pull your free reports at AnnualCreditReport.com and check that the late shows correctly as 30 days, dated November 2024, on each one.

cases.message: When will my Credit Builder payments start showing on my credit report? And should I also get a secured card?

routing.reason: The member asks when Credit Builder payments are reported, which is credit-builder-account, and whether to also get a secured card, which is secured-card.

cases.reply:
**1. When your payments show up**

They should already be showing. Your profile shows 4 on-time Credit Builder payments, most recently on October 1. Each payment is reported to Equifax, Experian and TransUnion as an installment account (fixed payments with a set end date). Reporting happens monthly, a few days after the payment posts. Your VantageScore 3.0 of 612, up from 603 in September, shows your plan is already on your report.

A lender found no FICO score for you in September. FICO needs at least one account open 6 months or more and at least one account reported in the past 6 months. Your plan opened in June, so you haven't met the 6-month minimum yet. Keep paying on time to stay on track.

**2. Should you get a secured card?**

It can be a reasonable next step, but it's your call. Right now your only account is the Credit Builder plan. A secured card would add a revolving account (a card you can use and pay down again). That lets you build a history of utilization, which means how much of your card limit you use.

Key facts:
- A refundable deposit of $50 to $2,000 sets your limit. That money is set aside and isn't available to spend.
- No hard inquiry to apply, and no annual fee.
- A variable APR (yearly interest rate) of 27.99% applies to balances you carry month to month. Paying in full avoids interest.
- Keeping your balance low and paying before the statement date helps your reported utilization.

It makes sense if you can spare the deposit and pay the full balance each month.

Next step: Make your November 1 Credit Builder payment on time.

cases.message: Will my reported rent help me get a mortgage in 2027? And does my auto loan count toward my utilization?

routing.reason: The member asks two things: whether reported rent will help a mortgage (rent-reporting) and whether an auto loan counts toward utilization (utilization, which covers whether a loan balance counts).

cases.reply:
**1. Will reported rent help with a mortgage in 2027?**

It might, but that depends on the lender. Your profile shows 4 months of on-time rent reported since you enrolled in June, with no past rent added. The app reports rent to TransUnion and Experian, not Equifax.

Whether rent counts depends on which score the lender uses:
- **Classic FICO** (older versions many mortgage lenders use) ignores rent.
- **VantageScore 4.0** can count it. Since September 2026, any approved lender for loans sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac may choose it.

Your current score is 641 on VantageScore 3.0, a model that can count rent. That doesn't tell us what a mortgage lender will use, and no one can promise approval or that a lender will count your rent.

If you want more history on file, you can add up to 12 months of past rent for a one-time $25 fee. Your lease started in September 2024. That would add positive history, but it isn't a guaranteed score change.

**2. Does your auto loan count toward utilization?**

No. Utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) only includes revolving accounts like credit cards. Your auto loan is an installment loan, so it isn't part of it.

Your profile shows utilization at 22%: $550 on a $2,500 limit, all on your bank credit card. That's under the common 30% guideline. Under 10% tends to be better. Paying the card down before the statement closing date lowers the balance that gets reported.

Next step: When you start talking to mortgage lenders, ask each one which credit score model and which bureaus it uses.

cases.message: Should I pay the $1,200 phone collection? And can your Debt Settlement service handle it?

routing.reason: The member asks whether to pay a $1,200 collection account, which falls under collections, and whether the Debt Settlement service can handle it, which falls under debt-settlement.

cases.reply:
**1. Should you pay the $1,200 phone collection?**

That's your choice. Here are the trade-offs for this account:

- **Paying won't remove it.** It would show as paid. It can stay on your report until about March 2029, seven years from the first missed payment on March 14, 2022. Paying doesn't change that date.
- **It may help some scores.** Your profile shows a VantageScore 3.0 score of 560. That model ignores paid collections. FICO 9 and 10 do too, but FICO 8, which many lenders use, still counts them. No one can promise a score change.
- **Watch the age of the debt.** Each state sets a deadline for suing over a debt, often 3 to 6 years. In many states a partial payment or a written promise to pay can restart that clock. Before you pay or promise anything, ask a legal aid office or attorney to check your state's deadline. This isn't legal advice.
- **Other free options.** You can ask the collector about a payment plan, talk to a nonprofit credit counselor, or reach our team at Help > Chat with support.

**2. Can Debt Settlement handle it?**

Yes, collection accounts qualify. Your profile shows you're already enrolled, with only the bank card listed.

- **Fee:** 20% of the amount saved. It's charged only after a deal is agreed and you make one payment under it. For example only, if $1,200 settled for $800, you'd save $400, pay an $80 fee, and pay $880 total. No outcome is guaranteed.
- **Limits:** Negotiating doesn't stop collection or lawsuits. A settled account still shows on your report.
- **Taxes:** Forgiven debt may count as taxable income. $600 or more forgiven usually triggers a Form 1099-C, but tax can apply even below that. Ask a tax professional.
- **Missed payments:** Your guidance doesn't say what happens if you miss a settlement payment. Support can tell you.
- **Free alternatives:** You can negotiate with the collector yourself or get help from a nonprofit credit counselor.

Next step: Call a local legal aid office to check your state's deadline before you pay or agree to anything on this debt.

cases.message:
Few questions:
1. Would rent reporting actually do anything for my score?
2. If I'm ever short on rent and it ends up with a collection agency, would paying it off later make it go away?
3. Once my secured card shows up, how long until I get my $300 deposit back?

routing.reason: The member asks three things: whether rent reporting affects their score (rent-reporting), whether paying off rent sent to collections makes it disappear (collections), and when they get their secured card deposit back (secured-card).

cases.reply:
**1. Would rent reporting help my score?**
It could, but it's not certain. The app reports on-time rent to TransUnion and Experian, not Equifax. Your profile shows a VantageScore 3.0 of 588, and that model can count rent. But your profile doesn't say which bureau that score comes from, so the effect varies. Lenders also pick their own models, and some, like FICO 8, ignore rent. It also won't remove or offset the September late payment. The cost is $4 a month, plus an optional one-time $25 to add up to 12 months of past rent.

**2. Would paying a rent collection make it go away?**
No. A paid collection (a debt sent to a collection agency) still shows on your report, marked as paid. It can stay up to 7 years from when you first fell behind, and paying doesn't restart that clock. Paying can still help with some scores. VantageScore 3.0, FICO 9 and FICO 10 ignore paid collections, while FICO 8 still counts them unless the original balance was under $100. The app never reports late rent, but a collector can. cases.message: thinking about cancelling my credit builder. if I do, do I get the $60 I've saved back right away so I can throw it at the store card? would closing it hurt my score or mess up my utilization? and since I got the store card current again on Oct 2, can I write them a letter asking them to take the 30 day late off

cases.reply:
**1. Getting your $60 back**

I can't tell you if the savings would come back right away, or how much, if you cancel early. Your profile shows $60 in savings, but I don't know how early cancellation handles it. Support can confirm this, and they'd also handle the cancellation itself, since I can't. (If you finish all 24 months, you get back $144 minus any unpaid amounts.)

**2. Would closing it hurt your score or utilization?**

It wouldn't change your utilization (how much of your card limits you're using). The plan is an installment loan, and those don't count in that ratio. Your utilization is 47%, and your store card alone is at 60% ($900 of $1,500).

Closing it can still matter. The account stays on your report with its 10 on-time payments, but it stops adding new on-time history and stops adding to your credit mix (having different types of accounts). Keeping it costs $6 a month, and your next payment is due Nov 1. Putting $60 toward the store card would bring it to about 56%. That's a small change.

**3. Asking them to remove the late payment**

Yes, you can send a goodwill letter. It asks the store card company to remove an accurate late payment as a courtesy. They don't have to agree, but it's reasonable to ask after a one-time slip that you've fixed. Paying on Oct 2 brought the account current, but it doesn't erase the late mark. If they don't remove it, it can stay up to 7 years from Aug 25, 2026. Its impact fades as it ages and your on-time payments build up. Autopay for at least the minimum can help prevent another late payment.

Next step: Ask support (Help > Chat with support) what happens to your $60 if you cancel early, before you decide.

cases.message: Can I use your Debt Settlement service on my Credit Builder plan so I end up paying less? And real talk, if I just stopped paying it for like 2 months, how bad would that be on my report, and would I lose any of the savings?

cases.reply:
**1. Debt Settlement on your Credit Builder plan**

No. Only accounts that are charged off (written off as a loss by the lender) or in collections qualify. Stopping payments to make it qualify would cost you far more in credit damage than you'd save.

A late payment can stay on your report for up to 7 years. Payment history is the biggest part of a FICO score, about 35%. This plan is your only account, so a late mark would stand out. It could also hurt the payment record you'll need when you first get a FICO score.

**3. Would you lose savings?**

Your profile shows $24 in savings so far. At the end of the 24 months, you get back $144 minus any unpaid amounts, so missed payments would reduce what you get back. If you cancel instead, I don't know what happens to savings already paid in. Support can tell you.

If $6 a month has become hard to manage, support can talk through your options. A nonprofit credit counselor can also help for free.

Next step: Contact support in the app at Help > Chat with support before November 1 to ask about your options.

cases.reply:
**1. Do your phone and electric bills count?**

Usually not on their own. Many phone and electric companies don't report on-time payments to the credit bureaus (the companies that keep credit reports). That's why this history is often missing even when you pay every month.

No. Debt settlement only works with accounts that are charged off (written off by the lender as a loss) or in collections. Your profile shows your auto loan ($9,800 balance) as open and current, so it doesn't qualify.

Your on-time auto loan payments help build positive history. If the payment ever gets hard to make, you can ask the lender about hardship options or talk to a nonprofit credit counselor.

cases.message:
Getting my credit ready for a mortgage in 2027, so a few things:
1) If a landlord ever sent unpaid rent to collections, would paying it off get it off my report?
2) Do my phone and electric bills help my credit the way my rent reporting does?
3) Should I pay my card down to $0 before the lender pulls my credit?

routing.reason: The member asks three things: whether paying off a landlord collection removes it (collections), whether phone and electric bills build credit (bill-reporting, distinct from their rent reporting), and whether paying a card down before a mortgage pull helps (utilization).

cases.reply:
**1) Paying off a rent collection**

No, paying it would not remove it. A paid collection still shows on your report, marked as paid. It can stay up to 7 years from the date you first fell behind, and paying doesn't restart that clock. Some score models ignore paid collections, including VantageScore 3.0, the model behind your score. FICO 8 still counts them. Your profile shows no collections, so this is general information.

**2) Phone and electric bills vs. rent**

Not right now. Your profile shows you aren't using Bill Reporting, and many phone and power companies don't report on-time payments themselves. The app's Bill Reporting is free. It reports on-time phone, utility and internet payments to Equifax only, and late bills are never reported. Your rent goes to TransUnion and Experian, not Equifax. Whether a lender sees bill payments depends on which bureau it pulls and which score model it uses.

**3) Paying your card to $0**

You don't need to hit $0. Your profile shows utilization (how much of your card limit you're using) at 22%: $550 of a $2,500 limit. Common guidance is to stay under 30%, and under 10% tends to be better. Forcing 0% brings no real benefit. Card issuers usually report your statement balance, so paying before the statement closing date lowers what gets reported. Under 10% on your card means a reported balance below $250. No one can promise how a score will change.

Next step: Check your card's statement closing date and plan to pay the balance below $250 before that date.

cases.message: Getting ready to apply for a mortgage sometime next year, so a few things: 1) Will the lender actually count my rent history? 2) Is there a way to see if I'd be approved for a Marketplace card without a hard inquiry? 3) If I pay my cards down to zero right before I apply, will the lender only see that, or do they look back at older balances too?

routing.reason: The member asks three things: whether a mortgage lender counts rent history (rent-reporting), whether they can check Marketplace card approval without a hard inquiry (marketplace-offers), and whether paying cards to zero before applying affects what a lender sees (utilization).

cases.reply:
**1) Will the lender count your rent history?**

It depends on which score and credit bureaus the lender uses. Your profile shows 27 months of rent on record: 15 reported since you enrolled, plus 12 past months added. The app reports rent to TransUnion and Experian only, not Equifax.

For mortgages sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, lenders can use Classic FICO, which ignores rent, or VantageScore 4.0, which can count it. Since September 2026, any approved lender may choose VantageScore 4.0. So rent counts only if your lender picks a model that uses it.

**2) Checking a Marketplace card without a hard inquiry**

Some issuers offer prequalification. This is usually a soft inquiry (a check that doesn't affect scores). Prequalification is not approval, and the app doesn't know your approval odds. A full application usually triggers a hard inquiry (a check that can affect scores), and a new account will show up when your mortgage lender reviews your report. Marketplace partners may pay the app when a user is approved.

**3) Paying cards to zero before applying**

Most scores look only at the balances reported now. Trended-data models also look at up to 24 months of balance history. These include VantageScore 4.0 when trended data is used, and FICO 10T, which isn't yet usable for these mortgages.

Your utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) is 12%, and both cards are at 12% on their own. Under 10% tends to be better, but zero isn't needed. Paying before your Secured Card statement closes on the 10th lowers the balance that gets reported.

Next step: Ask a mortgage lender which score model and bureaus it uses.

cases.message: ok a few things. first, my rent is showing on my TransUnion report but my phone, electric and internet bills aren't, is something broken? second, my score went from 695 to 702 this month, any idea why? and third, I'm moving in the spring, so if the final electric bill slips through the cracks, does it even matter since you only report on-time bills anyway? like if it ended up in collections and I paid it later, would it come off?

routing.reason: The member asks three things: why rent shows on TransUnion but utilities don't (bill-reporting covers Equifax-only utility reporting; rent-reporting covers which bureaus get rent), why the score rose 695 to 702 (score-changes), and whether an unpaid final electric bill in collections would come off once paid (collections).

cases.reply:
Good questions. Here's each one.

**1. Bills not on TransUnion**
Nothing looks broken. Bill Reporting sends your phone, electric, and internet payments only to Equifax. Rent Reporting goes to TransUnion and Experian. So seeing rent but not bills on TransUnion is expected. Your profile shows all three bills with 8 months reported each. Check your Equifax report to see them. If they're missing there too, contact support at Help > Chat with support.

**2. Score from 695 to 702**
Your profile shows a VantageScore 3.0 of 702, up from 695 on September 15. I can't point to one exact cause. You have no negative items, no hard inquiries (credit checks when you apply) in the last 12 months, and utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) at 12%, which is $300 of $2,500. You also added more on-time payments on your Secured Card, Credit Builder, and rent. Any of these may have helped. Small moves like this are normal from month to month.

**3. A missed final electric bill**
Yes, it matters. The app never reports late bills, but the electric company can still send an unpaid bill to collections on its own. A collection can stay on your reports for up to 7 years. Paying it later won't remove it; it would show as paid. Some models, like VantageScore 3.0 and FICO 9, ignore paid collections. FICO 8, which many lenders use, still counts them unless the original balance was under $100. Paying the final bill on time avoids all of this.

cases.message: Is my credit card utilization too high right now?

routing.reason: The member asks whether their credit card utilization is too high, which is directly covered by the utilization skill.

cases.reply:
Yes, it's higher than common guidance suggests. Your profile shows overall utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) at 47%: $1,410 of $3,000 in limits. Common guidance is to stay under 30%, and under 10% tends to be better.

**Card by card**
Scoring models also look at each card on its own:
- **Retail store card:** $900 of $1,500, or 60%. This is the one that stands out.
- **Bank credit card:** $510 of $1,500, or 34%. This is a little above 30%.

Your balances went up from $900 (30%) the month before. Your Credit Builder plan doesn't count here because it's an installment loan, not a card. Your Secured Card hasn't arrived yet. Once you use it, its balance will count too.

**What can help**
- **Pay before the statement closing date.** Card companies usually report your statement balance, not what you owe on the due date. Your profile doesn't show your closing dates, so check each card's statement or app.
- **Pay more than once a month** to keep the reported balance low.
- **Keep your older cards open.** Closing one removes available credit and can raise your ratio.
- **A limit increase** would lower your ratio. Some companies do a hard inquiry (a credit check that can affect your score) for this, so ask first.

Under most current scoring models, high utilization stops weighing on your score once a lower balance is reported. That usually happens after the next statement. Your overall score still depends on everything else on your report.

Next step: Look up the Retail store card's statement closing date and plan a payment a few days before it.

cases.message: If I pay the $1,200 collection, will you guarantee it gets deleted from my report? I heard about pay for delete.

routing.reason: The member asks about pay-for-delete on a $1,200 collection, which falls under collections (paid collection effects, pay-for-delete), and the guarantee question about whether paying removes it is also covered there.

cases.reply:
**No, I can't promise that paying will get the collection deleted, and no one else can either.** Paying a non-medical collection like this one doesn't remove it. Your report would show it as paid instead. "Pay for delete" means asking the collector to remove the entry in exchange for payment. A collector may agree or refuse, so it's not something to count on.

**When it leaves your report:** Your profile shows the original missed payment was March 14, 2022. A collection can stay up to 7 years from that date, so expect it to drop off around March 2029, whether you pay it or not. Paying doesn't restart that clock.

**How paying could still help:** Your profile shows a VantageScore 3.0 of 560. That model ignores paid collections. FICO 8, which many lenders use, still counts them. So paying may help with some scores but not all, and I can't predict by how much.

**One caution before you pay:** This debt is over 4 years old. Each state sets a deadline for suing over a debt, often 3 to 6 years. In many states, even a partial payment or a written promise to pay can restart that deadline. A legal aid office or attorney can tell you your state's rule. This is general information, not legal advice.

If money is tight, you can ask the collector about a payment plan, or talk with a nonprofit credit counselor. You can also reach our team in the app at Help > Chat with support.

Next step: Call a local legal aid office to check your state's deadline before you pay or promise anything to the collector.

cases.message: If I pay off my Rewards card today, how many points will my score go up?

routing.reason: The member asks how much their score will rise by paying off a credit card today, which is a question about revolving balances and how they are reported, so the utilization skill applies; the question of how fast a score rises by paying down cards is covered by utilization.

cases.reply:
I can't tell you a number of points. No one can predict that, because your score depends on your whole credit report. But paying off your Rewards card is likely one of the strongest moves you can make right now, and here's why.

Your profile shows your utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) at 85%: $2,550 of $3,000. Common guidance is to stay under 30%, and under 10% tends to be better. Each card also counts on its own:

- **Rewards card:** $1,900 of $2,000, or 95%
- **Bank card:** $650 of $1,000, or 65%

If you paid off the Rewards card, your overall utilization would drop to about 22% ($650 of $3,000). That would put you under the 30% guideline, and your most maxed-out card would be at 0%. Your score went from 668 to 655 last month, after your balances rose from 70% to 85% following the car repair. So lowering balances goes right at the likely cause.

**Timing matters.** Card companies usually report your statement balance, not your balance on the day you pay. Your score won't reflect the payoff until a lower balance is reported, usually after your next statement. Paying before the statement closing date helps the lower number get reported sooner. Most current scores look only at your latest reported balances. So once a lower balance shows up, the high balance usually stops weighing on your score.

Next step: Check your Rewards card's statement closing date and make your payment before that date.

cases.message: Can I put a higher income on a Marketplace card application so I'm more likely to get approved? I really want my first card.

routing.reason: The member asks whether to inflate income on a Marketplace card application to improve approval odds, which falls under marketplace-offers (who approves offers, why Coach cannot give approval odds, and whether a new card fits their situation).

cases.reply:
No, please don't. Putting a higher income than you actually have on a credit application is fraud, and I can't help with that. It can also backfire. You could end up with a limit you can't afford to pay down, and the issuer could close the account if it finds out.

The good news is that your real record is a solid start for a first card:

- **Your score:** Your profile shows a VantageScore 3.0 of 612, up from 603 last month.
- **Your payments:** You've made 4 on-time Credit Builder payments with no late ones.
- **No recent applications:** You have 0 hard inquiries (credit checks from applying) in the last 12 months.
- **Your history is new:** Your oldest account opened in June 2026, and a lender found no FICO score for you in September. Some issuers look at FICO, so a short history can make approval harder.

With a stable profile like yours, applying with your true income can be reasonable. Know the tradeoff first. Applying usually triggers a hard inquiry, which can lower your score a little, and approval is never guaranteed. Coach can't tell you your approval odds. Marketplace partners may pay the app when a user is approved.

Some issuers offer prequalification. It's usually a soft check that doesn't affect your score, but it is not an approval. If you're turned down, the issuer must tell you why or tell you how to get the reasons.

Next step: Open the card offers you browsed, check which ones offer prequalification, and compare their fees and terms using your real income.

cases.reply:
I'm sorry about your job. That's a lot to handle at once, and calling early gives you the most options.

**Call the store card company before the due date**

Your profile shows the Store card is open and current, with a $280 balance on an $800 limit. You paid it on time on October 1. Ask the company if they offer a hardship program or payment plan. These can lower or pause payments for a while. Every company has its own rules, so ask what it would mean for your account and your credit report.

**If you can, pay at least the minimum**

The minimum is the smallest payment the company accepts to keep you current. Even paying just that keeps the account current. If you can't, know that companies usually report a payment as late only once it's 30 or more days past due. A few days late may bring a fee, but usually no late mark. I don't see your due date or minimum on file, so check your statement or the card's app.

**Get free or low-cost help**

A nonprofit credit counselor can help you build a budget and talk with creditors for you. You can also reach our human support team in the app at Help > Chat with support, or at support@example.com.

Losing a job happens to many people. It says nothing about who you are. Staying in touch with the company now protects your on-time history.

I'm sorry about your job. That's a lot to handle, and there are steps that can protect your credit while you get through it.

Your profile shows your Store card is current, with a $280 balance, and you paid it on time on October 1. That gives you some room to plan before the next due date.

**What to do now**
- **Call the Store card company before the due date.** Tell them you lost your job and ask about a hardship program or payment plan. Some creditors may lower or pause payments for a while, though they don't have to agree.
- **Pay the minimum if you can.** Even a small minimum payment keeps the account current. If you can't, know that creditors generally report a payment as late only once it is 30 or more days past due. Paying a few days late may cost a fee but usually doesn't add a late mark.
- **If you do fall behind, try to catch up before 30 days.** Late marks are reported in steps (30, 60, 90 days), and each step is more serious. A reported late can stay on your report for up to 7 years.
- **Talk to a nonprofit credit counselor.** They can help you build a budget around your new income and look at all your bills together, often at low or no cost.
- **Reach a person here** in the app at Help > Chat with support, or email support@example.com.
